target_customer: individual consumers who want a private daily journal with little effort; premium plan reported at $48 a year
problem: People intend to keep a journal but quit because opening an app is friction. OhLife emailed a daily prompt so that replying to the email wrote the entry.
business_model: freemium consumer subscription (premium reported at $48 a year by Kevin Kelly's Cool Tools review)

founders.name: Shawn Gupta
founders.background_notes: Listed as the founder on the YC page. Education and employers not found in sources opened.

exit.reason: Users received a shutting down email; no reason was found. Cool Tools lists the shutdown as October with a typo in the year.

technical_complexity.rationale: Scheduled email prompts plus inbound email parsing into a private archive is modest engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Years of accumulated entries created some lock in for users, but the mechanic itself was easy to copy.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent targeted it; the service ran for years before closing.

market_need_then: Public blogging platforms like LiveJournal and Blogger existed, and TNW in 2010 contrasted OhLife with them as a private alternative. Direct spend data was not found.

branding.domain_note: ohlife.com exact match; the host did not resolve when fetched.

identity.voice_and_tone: Conversational daily prompt, how did your day go

branding.brand_signature: The nightly email asking how your day went
branding.community_and_virality: Covered by TechCrunch and TNW, praised by Kevin Kelly, and a long time user wrote that they answered the prompt for four years before the shutdown email.

brand_strength.rationale: Strong user loyalty and press, and the nightly email ritual was the brand; but it never became a large consumer brand.

outcome_analysis: OhLife built a loved daily journal around one simple email ritual and kept loyal users for years, with press from TechCrunch and TNW. It shut down later, with users told by email, but no source gives the cause or an exact date, so no failure factors are assigned. A small team and a modest paid plan fit a lifestyle product that may not have grown enough for venture scale, though this is not stated by any source.
notes: Shutdown year is unverified: the Cool Tools page says October 2104, a typo, on a review dated January 2014. Competition list left empty because Penzu (2008) was only confirmed through an undated page. Penzu and 750 Words came up in search.
